# Pipa Agent Guide

Architecture, request flow, file ownership: [`docs/repository-overview.md`](docs/repository-overview.md).

Setup, checks, contribution, release process: [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md).

## Runtime

- Socket profile connects Slack to OpenCode. Managed profile runs OpenCode only.
- One Slack thread maps to one persisted OpenCode session.
- Different threads run concurrently. V2 messages use native steering; v1 retains same-thread interrupt-and-replace.
- Superseded turns must not persist stale state, post stale output, or add success reactions.
- Shutdown rejects new work and drains local observers/callbacks before disconnecting Slack. V1 aborts its server-side turns; v2 does not interrupt independently continuing native sessions. Owned OpenCode processes still stop; attached servers stay running.
- Attached OpenCode servers are health-checked, never process-owned.
- V2 follows native session responses beyond the first reply. Do not add turn-ownership policy or a second execution/recovery journal over OpenCode.
- V2 execution failures use OpenCode's message text. Do not add provider-error classification, recovery advice, or another sanitization layer.
- Runtime stays plain ESM. Prefer Node APIs and existing dependencies.

## Security

- Never expose Slack tokens through child environments, errors, logs, fixtures, or commits.
- Never commit local Pipa state.
- For v2, the configured directory is a starting location, not session confinement. Follow native session identity and ancestry across moves; keep Slack authorization and artifact containment as integration boundaries. Access-control changes require security review and regression tests.
- Preserve attachment cleanup and filename sanitization. Incoming files are limited to 10 MiB each; outgoing artifacts retain the 10-file/100 MB per-file and response limits.
- Preserve artifact containment, symlink, identity, type, count, and aggregate-size checks.
- Never expose local artifact paths to Slack.

## Code

- Trace full caller path before changing shared orchestration.
- Keep logic in one function unless composable or reused.
- No preemptive single-use helpers.
- Prefer `const`, early returns, direct property access.
- Avoid unnecessary reassignment, destructuring, import aliases, star imports, and `else` after return.
- Keep helpers near callers. Comment surprising constraints, not obvious control flow.
- Add dependencies only when Node and installed packages cannot provide a small clear solution.

## Tests and PRs

- Behavior change needs focused regression test in owning suite.
- Test real implementation. Avoid copied production logic, broad mocks, and global patches.
- Concurrency changes cover same-thread replacement and cross-thread independence.
- Keep docs aligned with user-facing commands, config, Slack behavior, limits, and releases.
- Use `type(scope): summary` commits and PR titles. Keep PRs focused.
- Open issue before large architecture or behavior changes.
- Version bumps happen only for intended releases; update both package files.

# Verify Slack permission notices

This is deterministic application/adapter evidence, not live Slack authorization or rendering proof. Do not start a real Socket listener or read a private profile. The approved check needs no Slack/provider credentials, paid inference or remote app changes.

## Launch

From the Pipa checkout, use Node 22+ and installed dependencies (`npm ci` only if missing). No persistent app instance is needed: the existing Node tests launch the real init/start functions with isolated fixture state and replace outbound Slack transport. They shut down each created app.

## Doctor

Run `git status --short --branch`, `git rev-parse HEAD` and `node --version`. Check the intended revision and inspect `src/slack-permissions.mjs`'s capability map plus [the feature map](features/README.md). Never run `pipa start` against the operator's profile as a substitute for these tests.

## Drive

```sh
node scripts/verification/slack-permissions.mjs 2>&1 | tee /path/outside/checkout/slack-permissions.log
node --test test/app.test.mjs test/state.test.mjs
npm test
npm run test:pack
git diff --check
```

The focused suite must prove init/start notices and successful mention/follow-up delivery, not merely call a formatter. It also exercises the pinned adapter's real status method with controlled outbound APIs, metadata ID fallbacks and unchanged default manifest grants. See [permission notices](features/permissions.md) for the observable contract.

The capture command executes production `initializePipa`/`startPipa`, saving and loading configuration in the existing disposable runtime fixture. It prints actual notices through the injected warning sink and captures fake outbound posts, asserting healthy silence, core loss, optional/private loss copy/order, and mention/subscribed delivery through rejected status/reactions. Auth, Chat ingress and executor are injected; this is not a full Socket CLI start. Package smoke separately exercises actual CLI init and Managed start. Use a clean committed checkout for revision-bound evidence; the capture labels dirty development runs.

## Evidence

Save command output outside the checkout in the run's approved temporary evidence directory. Record the exact commit, dirty diff if any, Node/OS, command, exit status and test totals. Rerun affected checks after review cuts; record final-head GitHub CI separately. No token values, profile JSON or raw authenticated responses belong in evidence. Inspect terminal messages in the notice tests/README for the approved consequence-and-remedy format.

## Cleanup

Tests own and stop their fixture app instances; no live listener or production profile is created. Retain the terminal logs and revision record after tests finish. Do not delete unrelated temporary files or kill processes by name. A hung test is a failure to diagnose, not permission to restart production Pipa.

Pipa turns OpenCode into a Slack agent. Start sessions and talk to OpenCode from Slack.

Watch the four-minute setup video · How it works · Contributing · Issues

> **Early preview.** Features may break. Commands, configuration, and Slack behavior may change. If Pipa is useful, [star the repo](https://github.com/lunchpaillola/pipa). ## Why Pipa | What it does | What that means | | --- | --- | | **Thread sessions** | Mention Pipa to start a session. Reply in the thread to keep working. | | **Routines** | Schedule work in your timezone. Send results to a channel or thread. | | **Access control** | Choose which Slack channels, people, and bots can use Pipa. | ## Pipa for Teams Pipa is free and open source. [Pipa for Teams](https://www.usepipa.com/teams?utm_source=github&utm_medium=repo_readme&utm_campaign=teams&utm_content=readme) is an optional service for organizations: deployment and configuration for agreed workflows using supported integrations, plus training and handover. ## Quickstart **Runs on** macOS, Linux, and Windows. **Requires** Node.js 22 or newer, [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) installed and authenticated, and a Slack workspace where you can create an app. ```sh npm install --global @usepipa/pipa@0.6.0 pipa init pipa start ``` `pipa init` walks you through Slack setup and saves your profile under `~/.pipa`. Invite Pipa to an allowed channel and mention it. Follow the [four-minute setup video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rlTMdkPWPcA) or the [written tutorial](https://www.usepipa.com/opencode-slack?utm_source=github&utm_medium=repo_readme&utm_campaign=signup&utm_content=readme_install_guide). ### Install with your agent Paste this into your coding agent on the computer where Pipa will run: ```text Help me install Pipa Local. Check prerequisites and whether a Pipa profile already exists. Inspect only non-secret configuration fields; never print or return credentials in tool output or chat. Ask me to complete Slack authentication and app setup myself; never ask me to paste tokens into chat. For a new installation, follow https://www.usepipa.com/install. For an existing profile, do not run pipa init: use the README's upgrade instructions, explain the steps and ask me before making changes, and back up the profile first. ``` ### OpenCode version selection Pipa automatically detects OpenCode v1 or v2 and selects its native adapter. There is no manual Pipa migration command. OpenCode owns its data/schema upgrades; installing Pipa does not install or upgrade OpenCode. Unversioned installs use npm's `latest` tag; `@beta` selects the beta channel. Before upgrading, stop/drain Pipa and back up its profile. Keep your current OpenCode version initially. Do not rerun `pipa init` or start a second listener. Read the [release notes](docs/release-0.6.0.md) for limits and rollback steps. ## Security model Pipa runs locally by default. Its OpenCode server listens on `127.0.0.1`; attached servers use their own network controls. Slack allowlists control who can send requests. Empty channel and human-user lists allow everyone otherwise eligible. Other bots are blocked unless listed. **The working directory is a starting location, not a sandbox.** Allowed users can ask the agent to use the OpenCode profile's tools and permissions beyond that directory. Set channel and user allowlists before sharing Pipa. Slack tokens stay in the local profile with private file permissions. OpenCode manages provider credentials. Keep tokens, passwords, and local state out of shared output and commits. Read [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for security boundaries and reporting. ## Local Socket Mode Socket Mode connects Pipa to Slack through an outbound connection. You do not need a public web endpoint. ### Install 1. Install Pipa: ```sh npm install --global @usepipa/pipa@0.6.0 ``` 2. From the folder where you want Pipa to work, run: ```sh pipa init ``` Follow the prompts to create and install the Slack app. Choose your working directory and set channel and user allowlists. 3. Start Pipa: ```sh pipa start ``` Keep `pipa start` running. Invite Pipa to an allowed channel and mention it. Replies in that thread continue the same session without another mention. Different threads work independently. On OpenCode v2, replies steer ongoing work, and background results can return to the thread. V1 interrupts the current turn when a new message arrives. Replies missed during a disconnect or restart are not recovered. After restart, send another message in the thread to resume background forwarding. Failed Slack deliveries are not replayed. Pipa sends only your current request, attachments/full links, and Slack channel/thread identity to OpenCode. It does not automatically fetch or inject earlier Slack messages, even for a new or replacement session. Existing OpenCode sessions retain their own conversation history. When earlier context is needed, the agent can explicitly read the Slack thread using its available Slack tools; old messages are context, not fresh permission to act. On v2, Pipa tries to continue the saved conversation normally. If OpenCode explicitly rejects the prompt because that session's working folder is missing, Pipa queues a native move to the configured starting folder, waits for the location to change, then resubmits that rejected request once. OpenCode owns active and queued work; Pipa does not veto, clear, or replay it. A short Slack heads-up is best-effort and never required for continuation. Missing files are not restored. Transport-uncertain requests are never automatically replayed. Startup, stop, and restart behavior are unchanged. Startup waits for OpenCode and Slack to be ready, with no default overall timeout. Ctrl+C stops startup and processes Pipa owns, not attached servers. See [OpenCode compatibility](docs/opencode-compatibility.md) for startup, session, and upgrade details. ### Slack permissions The generated manifest requests the out-of-box experience, **not a minimum set of mandatory permissions**. `pipa init` and `pipa start` explain missing capabilities from the bot token's reported grants, without blocking startup: ```text ✖ ERROR — Pipa cannot send text replies. Ask your Slack app admin to grant chat:write (bot) to enable replies. ⚠ WARNING — File uploads unavailable. To enable uploads, ask your Slack app admin to grant files:write (bot). ``` ERROR means a core path is unavailable; WARNING means an enhancement or channel-specific capability is unavailable. Each notice connects the consequence to its fix. Related private-channel follow-up/context losses share one notice. A single “Still available” line may identify unaffected public-channel text capabilities based on the reported scopes; it is not a live connection or provider test. The subsequent Socket Mode connection message does not establish that replies or every feature work. Healthy grants produce no permission checklist. Missing `assistant:write` alone produces no notice when `chat:write` is present. Extra grants and scopes Pipa does not use are ignored. If scope metadata is unavailable or unusable, the existing check stays silent rather than guessing that permissions are missing. An actual authentication, Slack operation or OpenCode/provider error is separate; adding an optional Slack scope does not fix a provider/model failure. #### Requested scopes and actual use All links below describe current official Slack permissions. This audit covers Pipa and its pinned Slack adapter, not independently configured OpenCode tools or MCP integrations. “Required” applies to the named path, not every possible entry point. The xoxb bot token supplies all bot rows; Slack may also support these scopes on other token types. | Scope | Token | Requirement and impact when absent | | --- | --- | --- | | [connections:write](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/connections.write/) | App-level (`xapp-`), requested separately during setup | **Core Socket Mode:** required to open the event connection. Not a bot scope. Managed profiles need no Slack permissions. | | [app_mentions:read](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/app_mentions.read/) | Bot | **Core mention-event path:** allows the subscribed `app_mention` event. Without it that event path is unavailable; channel message subscriptions are separate entry paths. | | [chat:write](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/chat.write/) | Bot | **Core replies:** sends text replies and interaction feedback. Without it Pipa cannot post ordinary replies. Also authorizes current processing-status calls. | | [channels:history](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/channels.history/) | Bot | **Public-channel experience:** receives `message.channels` events and permits explicit public-thread reads. Without it unmentioned public-channel follow-ups are unavailable; new mention events are a separate path. | | [groups:history](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/groups.history/) | Bot | **Private-channel experience:** the equivalent dependency for `message.groups` and explicit private-thread reads. Does not affect public-channel history. | | [commands](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/commands/) | Bot | **Optional model slash commands:** required for this entry point, not ordinary mentions/replies. Matching command registration and interactivity are also needed. | | [files:read](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/files.read/) | Bot | **Optional incoming files:** the adapter downloads private attachment URLs using the bot token. Missing access can fail an attachment-bearing request; plain text does not need it. | | [files:write](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/files.write/) | Bot | **Optional outgoing files:** the adapter uploads artifacts and full-form details. Artifact delivery has a text-only fallback, not a guarantee that every file-dependent interaction works. | | [reactions:write](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/reactions.write/) | Bot | **Optional receipt/result reactions:** eyes/success/failure reactions are best-effort: rejections are caught, but a slow or pending receipt reaction can delay the reply because Pipa awaits it before enqueueing the turn. | | [channels:read](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/channels.read/) | Bot | **Optional public-channel names:** adapter `conversations.info` lookups resolve channel references; denied lookups fall back to IDs. Not required for every text reply. | | [groups:read](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/groups.read/) | Bot | **Optional private-channel names:** the corresponding metadata permission; denied lookups fall back to IDs. | | [users:read](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/users.read/) | Bot | **Optional user names/profiles:** adapter `users.info` lookups enrich authors and mentions. IDs remain available for Pipa authorization. Email access is not requested. | | [assistant:write](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/assistant.write/) | Bot | **Transitional alternative for processing status**, not required for ordinary replies or a prerequisite for DMs. Pipa currently calls only `assistant.threads.setStatus`; `chat:write` already satisfies that method. | | [files:read](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/files.read/), [files:write](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/files.write/) | User (`xoxp-`), generated user grants | **Unused by Pipa's runtime:** Pipa accepts app/bot tokens, not a user token. These user grants do not authorize its bot downloads/uploads. The generated defaults are retained; Pipa does not automatically remove grants. | As checked on November 16, 2026, Slack's [status-method documentation](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods/assistant.threads.setStatus/) and [scope-update changelog](https://docs.slack.dev/changelog/2026/03/05/set-status-scope-update/) allow **`chat:write` OR `assistant:write`**. Slack explicitly describes the latter as transitional and plans to accept only `chat:write`. Do not rely on it as a lasting alternative. Pipa keeps its existing best-effort typing call and default manifest; failed status calls do not block replies. The pinned adapter's comment about requiring `assistant:write` and the assistant split view predates this Slack change. This is documentation/contract evidence, not a live Slack rendering test. Pipa does **not** request [canvases:read](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/canvases.read/) or [canvases:write](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/scopes/canvases.write/), or invoke canvas APIs. The adapter can recognize a canvas ID, but that is not canvas content support. No canvas permissions warning is warranted. DMs remain excluded; granting `assistant:write` does not enable them. #### Enabling a capability Enable only the optional capabilities you want. Use `pipa manifest` to inspect the local template, then merge the desired scopes/commands into the **existing** Slack app; do not overwrite a customized manifest or rerun `pipa init`. If you change granted scopes, Slack may require installation/reauthorization. A package upgrade alone does not change app grants. Scopes alone are not sufficient: keep Socket Mode enabled, install/invite the bot to the intended channels, subscribe the matching events, and keep Pipa's channel/user allowlists correct. Private-channel access needs membership. Model slash commands also need matching definitions and interactivity; see [existing-installation upgrades](#upgrading-an-existing-installation). Scope metadata describes the bot token only, not app-level or user-token grants. App-token preflight remains separate and reports a required scope only for Slack's explicit `missing_scope` rejection. Permission notices are printed once per init/start invocation, not on each message or status attempt; no new logs or permission probes are added. ### Files Include a text prompt with attachments. Incoming messages allow up to 10 files, each at most 10 MiB. Temporary copies are removed after the turn. Your model must support the files you send. Generated files must stay inside Pipa's private artifact directory under `.pipa/artifacts`. Pipa checks paths, file identity, type, count, and size before sending them. Outgoing limits are 10 files and 100 MB per file or response. If file delivery fails, Pipa retries the summary without files. Attached servers on non-loopback hosts return inline text instead. Attached v2 servers may need `BUN_JSC_maxRegExpStackSize=536870912` in the **server process** to handle large attachments. Pipa sets this by default for v2 servers it starts, unless overridden. See [attachment guidance](docs/opencode-compatibility.md) for details. ### Access control By default, Pipa answers human users in channels it can see, excluding DMs and external channels. Use channel and user allowlists to restrict access. `pipa init` asks for these and saves them in the config: ```json { "botName": "Pipa", "workingDirectory": "/work", "slackAppToken": "xapp-...", "slackBotToken": "xoxb-...", "allowedSlackChannelIds": ["C0BSE2JTYPR"], "allowedSlackUserIds": ["UFWBSCZ54"], "allowedSlackBotIds": ["B0C6Q27E82X"] } ``` - Human requests must pass both the channel and user allowlists. Missing or empty lists allow all otherwise eligible channels or people. - Other bots are blocked unless listed in `allowedSlackBotIds`. Use the sender's `bot_id` (`B…`), not its app ID (`A…`) or user ID (`U…`). Bots must pass the channel list but do not need a user-list entry. - For scripted setup, use comma-separated `PIPA_ALLOWED_CHANNEL_IDS`, `PIPA_ALLOWED_USER_IDS`, and `PIPA_ALLOWED_BOT_IDS`. - Restart Pipa after editing the config. Access is checked again for each turn, interaction, and delivery. #### Mention-only mode Set `mentionOnly` to `true` to require an @-mention for every turn, even in an existing thread: ```json { "mentionOnly": true } ``` `pipa init` asks for this. For scripted setup, use `PIPA_MENTION_ONLY` (`1`, `true`, or `yes`). Missing or `false` keeps thread-following on. Routines are unaffected. #### Find the sender's bot ID Open the **sender app** at [Slack Apps](https://api.slack.com/apps). Under **OAuth & Permissions**, get its installed Bot User OAuth Token. Set it locally in `SLACK_SENDER_BOT_TOKEN`, then call [Slack `auth.test`](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods/auth.test/): ```sh curl --silent --show-error --request POST \ --header "Authorization: Bearer ${SLACK_SENDER_BOT_TOKEN}" \ https://slack.com/api/auth.test ``` Use the response's `bot_id` in `allowedSlackBotIds`. Keep the token out of config examples, shared output, and commits. **Incoming webhooks:** use the posted message's actual `bot_id`; it may differ from `auth.test`. Read it from the event or [conversation history](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods/conversations.history/) with the required access and history scope. Allowed bots still need to mention Pipa or reply in a subscribed thread. Webhooks must put the mention in `text`. Only allow bots whose messages you trust as agent requests. ### Use an existing OpenCode server Set the server URL before starting Pipa. Pipa checks the workspace but does not start or stop that server. If it requires authentication, also set `OPENCODE_SERVER_USERNAME` and `OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD`: ```sh export PIPA_OPENCODE_ATTACH_URL=http://localhost:5555 pipa start ``` **External clients of a Managed profile:** set an explicit shared `OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD` in the server/restart environment and every client. On v2, `OPENCODE_PASSWORD` takes precedence; match it or remove conflicting values. Otherwise Pipa generates a private password for each launch, and external clients cannot connect. Keep passwords private. See [OpenCode compatibility](docs/opencode-compatibility.md). ### Choosing a model In an allowed channel, type your app's command followed by `model`: `/chopper model` for `Chopper`, or `/pipa model` when registered. Search by model name, ID, or provider. Choose a model, save, and wait for the private confirmation. Cancel leaves the setting unchanged. The choice applies to new threads without restarting Pipa. Existing threads keep their model across replies and restarts. New routines save the current choice; existing routines keep theirs. Routines with no saved model use OpenCode's default. With no selection, new threads also use OpenCode's default. Changing this setting does not change subagents or external clients. To use a different model from Slack, save your choice and start a new thread. The picker does not change existing threads. The picker shows up to 100 matches; narrow your search for more. A listed model may still lack credentials or quota. Saving does not test it. Providers such as `opencode` and `openai` use separate credentials. If a provider fails, choose an available model and start a new thread, or ask your Pipa operator to reconnect it. [Connecting providers from Slack](https://github.com/lunchpaillola/pipa/issues/68) is a separate follow-up. Pipa never silently switches models. **Multiple Slack apps:** give each a distinct command. Slack sends a shared `/pipa` command to the most recently installed app. Register that alias with only one app, and check the app name in the picker before saving. ### Upgrading an existing installation **An npm upgrade does not update your Slack app, register commands, or grant scopes.** Mentions and thread replies still work without the model command. Do not rerun `pipa init` or replace credentials to add it. After verified publication, stop/drain Pipa and privately back up its profile before upgrading to `0.6.0`. Keep the current OpenCode version and use the same `PIPA_HOME` as your existing installation (leave it unset for the default `~/.pipa` profile): ```sh npm install --global @usepipa/pipa@0.6.0 pipa --version pipa manifest > "$HOME/pipa-slack-manifest-0.6.0.json" ``` `pipa manifest` prints a local template without tokens. It does not change your profile or contact Slack. It is not an export of your app's current Slack settings. 1. Open your **existing app** in [Slack App Management](https://api.slack.com/apps). Back up its current manifest. 2. Merge the desired `features.slash_commands` entries and add `commands` to `oauth_config.scopes.bot`. Keep existing settings, commands, scopes, Socket Mode, and interactivity. **Do not replace a customized Slack manifest with the local template.** 3. Save and reinstall or reauthorize the same app. Keep your tokens unless Slack rotates them. If it does, update the existing local config securely. 4. Start the same stopped profile with its existing launch environment: ```sh pipa start ``` Wait for readiness, then try the registered model command. The absence of a startup warning does not prove the command is installed. Renaming the bot in Slack does not update Pipa's `botName` or command registration; keep them aligned and restart. To try an unpublished branch, follow the isolated test-app steps in [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Never start a second Socket listener with a running installation's credentials. ### Routines Routines run scheduled work and send results to a channel or existing thread. Replies continue that session. Routines use the profile's directory, tools, permissions, and allowlists. Preview agent-assisted changes, check the JSON, and confirm before saving: ```sh pipa routine create \ --prompt "Send the daily brief" \ --timezone America/New_York \ --channel C0BSE2JTYPR \ --every 1d \ --times 05:00 \ --preview \ --json ``` Remove `--preview` to save. Use `--prompt-file` for exact multiline text or shell characters. Prompt files may be outside the starting folder; generated-file restrictions still apply. Use IANA timezones such as `America/New_York` or `UTC`, not `EST`. Supported schedules: ```sh # Every 30 minutes pipa routine create --prompt "Check the queue" --timezone UTC --channel C0BSE2JTYPR --every 30m # Once, five minutes from the CLI clock pipa routine create --prompt "Follow up" --timezone UTC --channel C0BSE2JTYPR --in 5m # Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday at three local times pipa routine create --prompt "Post status" --timezone America/New_York --channel C0BSE2JTYPR --every 1w --weekdays 2,4,6 --times 09:00,15:00,18:00 ``` Use `pipa routine list`, `show`, `edit`, `run`, and `delete`. Pause or resume with `edit --status inactive|active`. Completed routines stay until deleted. `routine run` requests one execution without changing the schedule or status. Routines need Socket Mode `pipa start` running and the machine awake. Missed scheduled runs are skipped. Explicit run requests survive restart, but a crash can cause repeated actions or deliveries. Managed profiles do not run routines. Use `pipa routine --help` for all options. ### Restarting Pipa Ask Pipa to restart, or run: ```sh pipa restart pipa restart --status ``` Anyone allowed by Slack user and channel controls can request a restart. ## Options and evidence

- `--pins=1.18.35,2.2.5` and `--modes=attached` select a smaller matrix.
- `--smoke` selects beta collection through the existing gate; `--pins`/`--modes`
  can narrow it. It rejects `--baseline`, `--migration` and `--gate` overrides.
- `--migration` seeds each v1 pin, stops its writers, snapshots the entire private
  profile, attempts continuation on native **2.2.5** on a disposable copy, and tests rollback on
  a separate pristine v1 copy. Omitting it leaves required migration evidence
  blocked. No existing user database is read or migrated.
- `--report=<private-json-path>` chooses the report location; its parent must
  exist. By default the command prints a unique report path in the OS temp area.

### Isolated Slack model smoke

Use a distinct Slack test app and a separate `PIPA_HOME` (the parent of `.pipa`), with its own app/bot tokens, working directory, and channel/user allowlists. Install the slash command derived from its configured `botName` (for example, `Chopper` -> `/chopper`) and grant `commands`. The generated manifest also suggests `/pipa`; omit that alias when another app already owns it, unless intentionally transferring that command. Enable Socket Mode and interactivity, reinstall or reauthorize, and invite the test app to the allowed channel. The generated manifest and runtime must use the same normalized name; a Slack app/bot rename alone does not update command registration or local config. Never run a second Socket listener with production credentials or restart production Pipa for a smoke test.

Isolate OpenCode HOME/XDG, database, configuration, and supported platform-specific storage paths separately; `PIPA_HOME` isolates only Pipa state. Migration rehearsals use stopped, matched Pipa/OpenCode snapshots and disposable copies, never the only copy of a real profile. Preserve existing profile files; v2 no longer uses the old recovery journal or gates intake on it.

1. Open the installation's model command (for example `/chopper model`), verify the loading window becomes a searchable picker, search by name/ID/provider and save model A, wait for the private saved confirmation, then reopen to verify the selection. With a large catalog, verify a model beyond the first 100 matches is searchable and remains selected on reopen. Closing the loading window must not reopen it when discovery finishes.
2. Send an ordinary request and inspect the completed OpenCode assistant message's provider/model metadata. HTTP acceptance or asking the model which model it is does not prove selection.
3. Save model B and reply in that same Slack thread. Verify completed metadata still names A and the session/history is retained. Start a new thread and verify it uses B. Restart the test profile and verify both threads retain their models.
4. Cancel another picker and verify no setting changed. Restart only the test profile and reopen to verify persistence.
5. Record selected IDs, completed metadata, and a short existing Slack conversation link separately from automated outcomes. Clean up only test-owned processes/state. Without the isolated app/profile, record the live-smoke gap rather than presenting adapter tests as live evidence.

Also check `mentionOnly`: unmentioned replies in subscribed threads are ignored when enabled and accepted when disabled; mentions still continue the same session. Routine create/preview must snapshot the selected default, and later default changes must not rewrite that saved model. During shutdown, pending model saves drain before Slack disconnects; accepted Socket event acknowledgments have a bounded drain after ingress detaches. For an existing profile, test `pipa manifest` as a read-only local-template export: credentials must be absent and config, sessions, routines, and cached manifest must remain unchanged. ## Releases

Pipa follows Semantic Versioning:

- New backward-compatible capability: minor release (`0.1.0` to `0.2.0`)
- Backward-compatible fix: patch release (`0.2.0` to `0.2.1`)
- Breaking change: discuss the version before release

### Controlled beta

An opt-in beta is a limited trial, not full stable/platform qualification. For
`0.6.0-beta.5`, use the [beta notes and publisher checklist](docs/beta-release.md).

1. Confirm the version is unused on npm and record the current `latest` tag.
2. Update both package files, beta notes and installation instructions in the PR.
3. Run `npm test`, `npm run test:pack`, and `node --test scripts/verification/self-check.mjs` on that exact version. Inspect `npm publish --dry-run --tag beta --access public` for package contents and accidental private data. Confirm Linux PR CI passes.
4. Record the scoped native smoke evidence and its platform/head limits. Retain known failures and gaps; do not label a beta `releaseQualified` or require the abandoned migration-status gate.
5. Obtain explicit owner approval for merge, release tag and GitHub prerelease. Merge only after required CI passes, then tag the actual merged commit as `v0.6.0-beta.5`.
6. The authorized publisher runs `npm publish --tag beta --access public` from that clean, versioned release checkout. Never omit `--tag beta`, move `latest`, or permanently set `publishConfig.tag` to beta.
7. Verify npm's `beta` tag points to the new version and `latest` is unchanged. Create the matching GitHub release marked **Pre-release**. Installation into an existing daily profile is a separate owner-approved cutover.

### Stable release

Except for the explicit 0.6.0 decision below, the stronger qualification requirements apply to future stable dual-engine releases:

1. Update `package.json` and `package-lock.json` in the feature pull request.
2. Run `npm test` and `npm run test:pack`. For this dual-engine candidate, also collect the full required Linux/macOS native OS/mode matrix, migration/rollback and private operator/live-client evidence. Windows native runs are outside the current scope; their absence alone does not block it. Missing required evidence still blocks release; the automated Slack collector alone cannot certify it.
3. Merge after CI passes.
4. Tag the merge as `v<version>` and push the tag.
5. The authorized human publisher runs `npm publish --tag latest --access public` from the clean, merged, tagged release commit.
6. Verify the published npm version, then create the matching GitHub release.

# Security

## Reporting a vulnerability

Do not open a public issue for a security problem. Email [help@lunchpaillabs.com](mailto:help@lunchpaillabs.com) with `Pipa security` in the subject, a description, reproduction steps, and the affected version. We will acknowledge the report and coordinate a fix and disclosure.

## Security model

Pipa is a local runtime. It has no hosted relay, database, public HTTP endpoint, or sandbox.

- The owned local OpenCode server binds to `127.0.0.1` on an operating-system-assigned port.
- Local mode starts and owns that server. An attached non-loopback server is externally owned and returns inline text instead of artifacts.
- Slack access is controlled by channel, human user, and bot allowlists. Every turn, interaction, and delivery rechecks the relevant limits.
- Slack tokens stay in the local profile under `~/.pipa` (or `PIPA_HOME`) with private file permissions. OpenCode manages provider credentials through its own credential store or provider environment variables. Pipa does not add credentials to Slack messages; upstream message text follows the boundary described below.
- Pipa reads generated files only from a private session directory under `.pipa/artifacts` in the configured starting directory. It validates path, type, identity, and size and limits delivery to 10 files and 100 MB. V2 retains that directory for background responses; v1 attempts removal after each turn. Native session moves do not relocate or widen this publication boundary.
- Incoming attachments are copied to a temporary directory for the turn, and Pipa attempts to remove it on every terminal path.
- Native v2 execution failures show OpenCode's message text, without provider-specific rewrites or an additional sanitization layer. OpenCode controls that upstream text; Pipa does not serialize attached response bodies or stacks into Slack messages. Existing Slack-token protection remains in the delivery path.
- Pipa never silently switches models.
- Slack prompt assembly passes only the current request, attachments/full links, and channel/thread identity; it never automatically reads or injects prior thread messages. Agents may explicitly read earlier messages through their available Slack tools when needed. Historical authors, bot replies, approvals and links are context, not fresh authorized requests. Slack authorization checks and read permissions remain in place. The existing adapter still owns Slack ingress and delivery.
- V2 missing-folder recovery keeps the mapped session and original artifact boundary. It uses native location resolution rather than assuming an attached server shares Pipa's filesystem. Recovery does not interrupt or clear observed pending work, restore files, or retry uncertain prompts. Native state reads are not atomic locks against other clients. Confirmed location changes are announced through the same authorized destination before the current prompt.
- The agent has the permissions of the OpenCode profile. In v2, the configured directory is a starting location, not a sandbox: native clients and agents can move sessions, including outside it. Pipa follows the mapped session and its descendants, never unrelated sessions. Invite the Slack app only to channels whose members may use that profile's full access.

## Supported versions

Security fixes target the latest published minor release. Upgrade with:

```sh
npm install --global @usepipa/pipa@latest
```

## Scope

In scope: token leakage, authorization bypass in Slack routing, path traversal or arbitrary file reads in artifact handling, command injection in the CLI or restart worker, and privilege escalation through the local profile.

Out of scope: the security of your OpenCode provider or model, your Slack workspace configuration, and the permissions you grant the agent in your own working directory.

# Pipa checks versus native OpenCode behavior

Pipa connects Slack to OpenCode. It should not invent execution failures for behavior OpenCode accepts. This review groups runtime/CLI checks by what they protect; it is not a claim that every error-construction site is a distinct policy or observed production incident.

## Removed in the native-v2 follow-up

- **Frozen session directory:** lookup, observer reuse, response-event filtering and child-interaction ownership no longer veto native moves. Session IDs and native parent relationships still select the Slack conversation. Reconnect uses session-scoped interaction reads, including independently moved descendants; a location-scoped global list cannot discover all of them.
- **Prompt echo veto after admission:** Pipa still sends the exact prompt once, but a successful native response no longer becomes a failed start because its returned representation differs. Genuine SDK/HTTP failures still propagate; Pipa does not automatically replay an uncertain admission.
- **Model catalog preflights:** native switching owns whether an explicit model is valid for a session. Browsing does not require a native-default read; resetting a session reads its current-location default directly, without catalog membership. Picker Save uses its authorized cached choice instead of rediscovering models.
- **Unused optional model validation:** config reads continue validating Slack access and required profile fields, but an invalid optional default does not veto authorization or an existing session with its own model. Defaults are normalized when actually used, and picker Save still validates the new selection.
- **Native error reinterpretation:** v2 execution failures use OpenCode's message text, without Pipa provider classification, recovery advice, or another sanitizer. SDK transport errors keep their existing representation. Pipa's default picker only affects new sessions.
- **Response/picker error replacements:** response reads, Slack delivery and model-picker failures retain the original error message instead of staged Pipa explanations. Only the existing Slack-token redaction applies; error bodies and stacks are not published. Failed partial response delivery is still not replayed.
- **V2 request deadlines and read recovery:** native requests use the SDK directly with caller/shutdown cancellation, without Pipa's request/body deadlines or timed read retries. Model discovery has no extra v2 deadline. Event attachment waits for a usable result path without a Pipa deadline; a stalled service can therefore keep it pending until cancellation or shutdown. Native event-stream reconnection remains separate from request replay.
- **Exact v2 CLI/server version equality:** different supported v2 versions no longer veto startup. Authentication, supported-major negotiation and the CLI/server major distinction remain; this is not a compatibility qualification for every v2 version.
- **Unused metadata and post-create directory checks:** unused v2 startup/catalog fields and directory spelling do not veto native success. Usable session identity and protocol negotiation still belong to the integration.
- **Explicit prompt-file confinement:** a local user-selected input file can be outside the starting folder or use a symlink. Relative resolution, bounded regular-file reading, and change detection remain; outbound publication has a separate boundary.

## Retained checks and concrete reasons

- **Slack access and interaction ownership** (`app.mjs`, `models.mjs`): prevent unauthorized requests, stale modal submissions and delivery after destination/responder revocation. Directory equality is not authorization.
- **Attachment and artifact validation** (`opencode.mjs`): prevent arbitrary file reads, symlink/path escapes, file replacement races and oversized uploads. Native moves do not change the original private publication directory.
- **Session identity and response shape** (`opencode-v2.mjs`, `opencode-v1.mjs`): prevent another session's data from reaching a Slack thread and avoid acting on malformed integration payloads. These do not impose a directory policy.
- **Credential-clean processes and existing Slack-token handling** (`opencode.mjs`, `app.mjs`): keep Pipa's Slack credentials out of child environments and its own diagnostics. Native v2 messages are not rewritten, except by the existing Slack-token protection in delivery; response bodies and stacks are not the message-text interface.
- **Startup protocol/authentication and starting-location checks** (`opencode.mjs`): establish that the selected server can serve the configured starting location. They do not confine an existing native session after startup.
- **Startup readiness probes and explicit harness deadlines** (`opencode.mjs`): remain separate from native execution requests, alongside caller cancellation and owned-process shutdown. Slack acknowledgment/UI-expiry timers and legacy v1 discovery limits are unchanged.
- **Observer readiness, cancellation and duplicate-delivery handling** (`opencode-v2.mjs`, `app.mjs`): avoid admitting work without an attached result path, posting after shutdown or replaying already-sent chunks. They are integration lifecycle checks, not native execution deadlines.
- **State, routine and process validation** (`state.mjs`, `routines.mjs`, `restart.mjs`, `bin/pipa.mjs`): protect persisted mappings, exact destinations, schedules, single-instance locks and owned restart handoffs. Removing them can lose continuity or target the wrong process/destination.
- **Permission and form translation** (`opencode-v2.mjs`, `app.mjs`): keep pending session forms in Slack, preserve typed native answers and explicit external-action acknowledgments, and leave controls editable when native submission fails. Slack authorization and native session ancestry still govern who can answer; opening an OpenCode client is not a fallback.

## Narrow missing-folder repair

V2 submits the current request normally. Only a prompt-time `LocationNotFoundError` matching the same session's current directory triggers one native queued move to the configured starting folder. Pipa waits for the native location to change, with caller/shutdown cancellation, then submits the definitely rejected request once using the same message ID and payload. It does not inspect or veto active or queued work. Normal folder switches remain valid, history and model identity are retained, and missing source files are not restored.

The short heads-up, “The old working folder is no longer available,” is best-effort: a failed or stalled Slack post does not gate continuation. Slack authorization is still checked before the recovered request continues. A pending native move is awaited, not treated as immediate failure. Native move failure, unrelated errors, retry rejection and transport uncertainty do not start another recovery attempt. V1 receives no new location-repair policy. Recovery remains separate from reconnect, response catch-up and process ownership.

## Deliberately separate legacy behavior

V1 still uses interrupt-and-replace, not v2's independent native steering. Failed admission or cancellation fails only the affected turn; it does not latch an installation-wide flag or stop the Slack listener. V1 does not resubmit prompts or automatically cancel native work just because an admission acknowledgement was lost. Same-session writer checks, native busy-status waiting, ordinary cancellation and stale-output suppression remain. A request connection/body-read failure is not evidence that the owned engine exited; actual process exit and explicit shutdown still stop Pipa.

## Evidence limits

HTTP/SSE fixtures exercise the shipped adapter and owning integration paths, including moved-session continuity and unrelated-session isolation. They are not a real-engine compatibility matrix or isolated live Slack smoke. This PR does not deploy, restart or publish Pipa.

### Startup contract

Ordinary OpenCode version probing, listening/readiness waits and Slack initialization
have no default overall startup limit, including no default 30-second cutoff.
Pipa detects v1/v2 and waits for native workspace readiness, not migration status:
it never calls `GET /api/experimental/migration/v1` at runtime. OpenCode alone owns
schema/data upgrades; Pipa never converts OpenCode data.

An explicit harness startup deadline is supported. Per-network-request safety
timeouts remain bounded and retry while waiting; terminal authentication, protocol
and wrong-workspace errors fail rather than retry indefinitely. Ctrl+C cancels
startup and stops an owned child; attached external servers survive.
Detached background restart and shutdown deadlines are unchanged.

Socket startup waits for native readiness before Slack subscriptions or routines.
Ordinary Managed startup can remain running without workspace readiness, but
cannot advertise cooperative restart readiness. A detached replacement must
pass its bounded readiness checks or report failure/unconfirmed status.

   the old package and engine pins. Review the qualification results for the
   intended candidate; a green package smoke alone is insufficient.
2. Stop/drain Pipa using commands on its host with the original `PIPA_HOME`.
   Confirm its owned server/writers have stopped before copying state. Attached
   servers are operator-owned and need their own writer coordination.
3. Snapshot the matched Pipa and OpenCode state as described below. Rehearse on
   isolated copies with the same working-directory identity before deployment.
4. Install the explicitly chosen Pipa candidate on the intended host; retain
   OpenCode v1 and the original Pipa profile. Do not rerun `pipa init` or recreate
   the Slack app just to change Pipa versions. Old profiles with no `slackMode`
   still load as Socket Mode.
5. Start the candidate with that profile, engine selection and directory.
   Verify a new mention, existing-thread history, permission/question controls,
   files, a routine/result-thread reply, and detached restart via the live gates.

Changing scopes is a separate Slack app reauthorization step, not a requirement
to create another app. Never run two Socket consumers for the selected app.

## Journey B: deliberately adopt v2

First complete Journey A's inventory, drain and matched snapshot. The Pipa
upgrade does not install or upgrade OpenCode automatically. The current synthetic
migration target is each pinned v1 release (**1.18.35 / 1.19.0**) to native
**2.2.5**; historical v1-to-2.0.29 reports remain historical evidence only.

1. Inventory required providers, credentials, MCP servers, file definitions and
   plugins privately. A required integration without a working v2 port blocks
   cutover. Renaming a plugin setting does not port its implementation.
2. Stop **all** writers to the source OpenCode storage, including independent
   clients/services. Copy the stopped complete profile/storage to a disposable
   target, leaving the pristine v1 snapshot immutable.
3. Select the exact **2.2.5** executable for the current qualification rehearsal in
   the candidate's private PATH, or select an
   independently managed v2 server. Preserve Pipa's config, session mappings and
   routine state; OpenCode owns schema/history migration. In this operator
   rehearsal, verify its upgrade completed and the configured location is ready
   before dispatching work; Pipa startup does not probe migration status.
4. Continue the same mapped sessions and recall pre-migration history. Inspect
   active/inactive/completed routine definitions, exact prompts and destinations.
   Restart v2 and repeat continuation. Do not treat a migration/auth/location
   error as a missing session or silently substitute a new conversation.
5. Verify configured permission rules. Upstream remembered approvals can reset
   during migration or service restart: expect new approval prompts where
   observed. Pipa neither recreates grants nor owns a separate approval store.
6. Complete the private operator checklist and actual Slack/client gates. Only
   after successful rehearsal and explicit deployment authorization should the
   production copies be migrated.

### Matched snapshots and rollback

`PIPA_HOME` is the parent of `.pipa`, not `.pipa` itself. Preserve the complete
stopped Pipa profile: config/manifest, `sessions.json`, `routines.json`, restart
records and `opencode-recovery.json` when present. Keep credentials private.
Preserve OpenCode's actual database/storage plus database companions, credentials,
configuration, definitions, plugins and their package sources from the same
checkpoint. Include project-local `.opencode` definitions/configuration too.
These matched backups protect the operator's OpenCode upgrade and session continuity,
not a Pipa-driven data conversion.

Discover paths from the selected release's CLI help/path commands and configured
HOME/XDG/Windows app-data/DB overrides; do not assume one universal DB path.
For qualified v2 HTTP identity, `/api/info` exposes paths. Never copy only a live
SQLite main file. Stop/checkpoint writers or use the release's documented
consistent backup procedure. Record version/path inventory and snapshot hashes
privately, without a full environment dump.

On failure, stop the new Pipa and all target-storage writers. Retain v2-written
data separately for diagnosis. Restore **both** pristine Pipa and OpenCode
snapshots and old package/engine selections into the original identity, then
verify the old sessions/routines/rules. Never open a v2-written database in v1.
Post-snapshot side effects and state changes need reconciliation; binary rollback
does not undo them. Do not delete recovery journals to bypass blocked intake.

The reproducible synthetic rehearsal is:

```sh
npm run test:engines -- --migration --gate=deterministic
```

This seeds each pinned v1 release with histories, mappings, routine states, configured deny
rules and a remembered approval; stops writers; migrates only a copy to native **2.2.5**; then
continues a separate pristine v1 rollback copy. It does not touch a live profile
or establish private operator/plugin compatibility.

## Configuration and deployment limitations

- Keep supported existing configuration/file definitions initially. V2 does not
  run LSP and ignores legacy `compaction.tail_turns`, `compaction.prune` and some
  experimental fields. Test workflows that depended on them; wholesale config
  conversion is outside this migration.
- V1 plugins require an actual compatible v2 implementation. Deterministic local
  definitions/MCP/plugin probes are separate from the operator's inventory.
  The [follow-up evidence](research/opencode-native-blockers-verification.md)
  corrects the synthetic v2 probes; it does not qualify installed operator plugins.
  V2 reads `plugins` (compatible package/directory entrypoints) and `mcp.servers`;
  MCP defaults to Code Mode, with `codemode:false` for direct tool exposure.
  Renaming keys alone does not convert plugin hooks or qualify credentials.
- Both v1 pins retain old plugin module bytes after location disposal. V1 plugin
  changes require a full native-process restart, not hot reload; this compatibility
  policy was approved on 2026-11-01 and verified with changed PID, retained history
  and exactly one updated hook. For attached servers, only the independent owner
  restarts the engine; restarting Pipa alone does not reload that engine's plugins.
  Their attached `run --command` can return
  before collecting output (an observed race); isolated standalone invocation returns it, but uses a
  separate session/process. The attached-command gate remains failed; historical
  hot-reload failures are retained, not relabeled as passes. V2 file commands
  work through `opencode api`/`session.command` plus completed-result collection;
  v2 `run --command` is not available.
- An attached server must serve the configured workspace and remain independently
  owned through Pipa stop/restart. Loopback attachment is not separate-host proof.
  Remote agent commands need access to the Pipa host for restart/routine CLI work.
- Incoming files are limited to **10 MiB each** against metadata and downloaded
  bytes. Owned v2 defaults `BUN_JSC_maxRegExpStackSize=536870912` unless overridden;
  independently launched attached v2 servers need that setting in the server
  process for the measured 2.0.29 large-base64 boundary. Model context/media limits
  remain separate. Outgoing files retain 10-file/100 MB per-file/response limits;
  non-loopback attachments use text fallback for local artifacts.
- V2 forwards live native session events beyond the first reply. Replies missed
  during disconnects or restarts are not recovered, and no response history is
  scanned. A fresh Pipa process restores conversation mappings and Slack
  subscriptions, not background observers; a new message reattaches that thread.
  Failed Slack response delivery is not replayed. Native message reads retain
  bounded transport retries; later live responses are not blocked by a failed post.
- Native 2.2.5's experimental session-log endpoint returned only `log.synced`
  during both live observation and replay in the isolated probe. Pipa therefore
  uses the working native event stream, not that endpoint.
- Background shell notices, restart notices and other native input do not cause
  Pipa attribution conflicts. New Slack messages use native steering rather than
  interrupting and replacing the OpenCode execution.
- Slack context is a stable native session instruction entry. The v2 adapter no
  longer creates per-turn temporary instruction entries or uses a recovery journal.
  Old journal files are left untouched and do not gate startup or other threads.
- Stopping Pipa detaches v2 observers and drains callbacks. An attached OpenCode
  server can continue its native work; stopping an owned server still stops that process.
- Ordinary HTTP requests remain bounded, but native event streams have no
  response-body execution deadline. Pipa sends each prompt through native admission;
  it does not independently reconstruct whether OpenCode executed it.
- Native permission rejection and question cancellation use their native replies;
  they do not require a journaled proof or a subsequent idle projection.
- Routine restart skips missed schedules; saved explicit run requests survive.
  A crash after side effects/delivery but before saving completion can repeat
  work. There is no new exactly-once promise.

# Pipa testing strategy

This is the reusable testing procedure for the dual-adapter candidate. The implementation plan's Verification Contract owns the detailed feature matrix and release gates, with its historical three-OS native requirement superseded by the [current Linux/macOS scope](opencode-compatibility.md#current-native-platform-scope). Windows native is `—` (not run), not a pass or a blocker solely because it is absent. Harness delivery and targeted native passes do not establish release qualification. See [compatibility and operator transition](opencode-compatibility.md) and the [U7 evidence](research/opencode-u7-verification.md).

## Three kinds of proof

1. **Deterministic:** `npm test` verifies implementation behavior, failure paths, concurrency, scheduling with controlled clocks, and process ownership. `npm run test:pack` verifies the installed npm package. PRs and pushes to `main` run these on Linux; maintainers manually dispatch **CI** for Linux/macOS/Windows checks on platform/process changes and before releases.
2. **Real OpenCode:** Qualify the exact CLI/client versions with isolated profile/database paths. Prove prompt admission versus final output, history migration, permissions/forms, attachments, cancellation, background work, and model switching against the real server.
3. **Real Slack:** Prove message routing, scheduled delivery, result-thread continuation, artifacts, and detached restart in the selected channel. An HTTP fixture cannot substitute for these round-trips.

Run the deterministic baseline before implementation. Record existing failures and compare after the change. Never describe unexecuted real-service checks as passed.

## Shared contract and pinned engine harness

Both adapters must pass the same semantic scenarios: exact prompts, session continuation, completion/error handling, question/permission lifecycle, cancellation, supersession, file handling, and cleanup. Native HTTP requests/responses/events use independent v1/v2 fixtures; expected data must not be generated by the adapter being tested. Version selection is exercised through the production facade.

Build the fixture contract and real-engine runner before the port. Record the current v1 baseline and current v2 failures rather than emulating a missing adapter. The harness-delivery step can finish with those named baseline incompatibilities; release qualification cannot. Rerun the identical production-path cases as the adapters and live evaluator land.

Harness ownership:

| Surface | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `test/helpers/runtime-fixture.mjs` | Private roots, controlled environment, direct child handles and ports, bounded teardown |
| `test/helpers/opencode-contract.mjs` | Shared product assertions independent of native endpoint spelling |
| `test/opencode-contract.test.mjs` | Both fixture generations in default `npm test` |
| `scripts/test-opencode-matrix.mjs` | Pinned real engines and installed Pipa tarball, with a deterministic local model |
| `scripts/verification/opencode-release-cases.mjs` | Shared production-path real-engine scenarios, outside default test discovery |
| `scripts/slack-release-eval.mjs` | Serial opt-in Slack/provider collection, shared live checklist, routine evaluator reuse, optional independent restart observation; human/integration gates remain blocked |

Keep the default `npm test`/`npm run test:pack` lane free of downloaded engines and live credentials. The opt-in `test:engines` lane exercises pins **1.18.35, 1.19.0, 2.0.29, and 2.2.5** against Socket-owned, Managed, and attached modes on Linux/macOS in the current release scope. Native **2.2.5** is the current v2 qualification target; **2.0.29** remains a historical comparison pin. The SDK remains `@opencode/client@2.0.29` pending real qualification. Pin inclusion does not claim passing native tests or release readiness; historical reports qualify only their recorded cases and versions. Node 22 is the baseline. The downloaded executable's identity and package integrity must match the selected cell; no global executable is replaced. Use `--migration` for synthetic upgrade/rollback. See [runner options](../scripts/verification/README.md).

Real engines are not part of automatic PR CI. Maintainers can manually dispatch
**OpenCode compatibility**, or run `npm run test:beta`, to check start, exact
prompt/history, restart and stop on 1.19.0 and 2.2.5 in three modes. This labelled
smoke is not full qualification; the broader matrix is also manual. See the
[beta scope](opencode-compatibility.md#small-beta-smoke).

Fixtures launch ordinary processes without a global spawn override or ownership
preload. Cleanup uses live child handles and explicit private-profile shutdown;
it does not reconstruct arbitrary orphan trees after their leaders exit.
Failed or uncertain cleanup retains the private root and fails the selected check.

The Socket-owned engine cell composes the real Pipa application, executor, scheduler and state with injected fake Chat/auth. Managed cells use the actual installed CLI and detached restart chain. Attached cells use an independently launched server and prove ownership preservation. Real Socket CLI restart and visible Slack controls still require the live lane; fake Chat does not prove them.

Mock only the model for deterministic real-engine cases. Drive real tool/question/permission flows and use stage barriers to force retries, lost responses, disconnections, revocation, and cancellation races. Tests must not impose their deadlines on valid production turns. Use controlled clocks for DST/long horizons and actual scheduler dispatch for short one-time/recurring runs.

Startup checks must cover v1/v2 detection and listening/workspace readiness plus
Slack initialization beyond 30 seconds without a default overall limit or runtime
migration-status request. Explicit harness startup deadlines may bound a test;
per-network-request safety timeouts retry, but terminal auth/protocol/wrong-workspace
errors fail. Ctrl+C must stop owned children and leave attached servers alive.
Detached background restart and shutdown deadlines remain unchanged. OpenCode owns
schema/data upgrades; the manual migration/rollback lane below is separate from
Pipa startup and does not authorize Pipa data conversion.

The former spike's 58 comparison checks and 55 routine/restart/CLI baseline passes are supporting evidence, not a substitute for running this harness on the implemented dual-adapter package.

## Isolate local state and recover migration failures

Each case gets private HOME/USERPROFILE, XDG config/data/cache/state, temporary directory, PIPA_HOME, workspace, artifacts, and supported engine database/config overrides. Isolate Windows app-data roots where used and retain required SystemRoot/ComSpec/PATHEXT plumbing. Construct child environments from an allowlist rather than inheriting the operator's credentials, attach URL, proxies, or Node options. Assert the product's intended non-Slack integration-variable inheritance separately with synthetic sentinels.

Generate synthetic old-version data with each pinned v1 engine (**1.18.35 / 1.19.0**). Stop/checkpoint it, preserve a pristine copy and needed database companions, then migrate only a disposable copy to native **2.2.5**, the current migration target. Continue the same session IDs/history and verify Pipa's thread mappings, routines, configured permissions, and documented remembered-approval reset. Restart 2.2.5 again. Rollback restores the matched old snapshot; it never opens v2-written data with v1. Historical v1-to-2.0.29 reports are not evidence for this target.

Force process death around context registration, prompt admission, pending approval, and completion. Pipa must clean up only its owned instruction/admission recovery state before accepting new work. Do not silently replay side effects or claim exactly-once delivery across crashes. The scheduler's existing crash-window semantics remain documented.

## Choose a live-test environment

Use a separate Slack test app and channel when available. Reusing an existing app is also supported: stop its existing Pipa process before another process uses the same Socket Mode credentials. The operator supplies app identities and the test destination through private configuration; this guide has no workspace-specific defaults.

- Verify the original process is stopped; a lock in a different `PIPA_HOME` does not prove that there is no other consumer of the same Slack app.
- Run the candidate from a separate private Pipa profile and disposable working directory. Restrict its channel allowlist to the test channel.
- Isolate OpenCode database and configuration too. `PIPA_HOME` isolates Pipa state, not OpenCode state. Use the qualified OpenCode release's supported path overrides.
- Supply app credentials through private profile configuration. Keep tokens out of command arguments, evidence, repository files, and agent child environments.
- Use a private snapshot for migration/rollback checks. Never run destructive migration experiments against the only copy of existing conversations or routines.
- When the run ends, stop its owned processes, record cleanup, and return control to the operator. Never leave two consumers of the app running.

## Evaluator inputs

Copy the committed `.env.example` to the gitignored `.env.test` and fill in the environment values for your workspace. Alternatively, inject the same environment variables from your shell or CI secret store. Do not add a second credentials-file format or a dotenv dependency.

The live entry point defaults to a side-effect-free checklist:

```sh
npm run test:slack:release -- --plan
```

For real execution, configure and start an isolated candidate first. `PIPA_HOME` selects its profile; its saved config contains the app/bot credentials. Restrict `allowedSlackChannelIds` to exactly the test channel. Isolate OpenCode HOME/XDG/Windows app-data/DB/config separately. Configure the intended real provider/model there; the evaluator does not change model preferences or automatically install/start a candidate.

Both evaluators use:

| Input | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `SLACK_TEST_CHANNEL_ID` | Exact destination selected by the operator |
| `SLACK_PIPA_BOT_USER_ID` | Identifies candidate Pipa replies |
| `SLACK_USER_TOKEN` | Existing human-message evaluation path |
| `PIPA_HOME` | Selects the candidate's private profile |
| `PIPA_TEST_SOLE_CONSUMER` | Set to `confirmed` only after stopping all other consumers of the selected app, including other hosts |
| `PIPA_TEST_ENGINE_URL`, `PIPA_TEST_ENGINE_PIN` | Exact serving URL and native version; authenticated identity/workspace preflight is read-only and does not inspect migration status |
| `PIPA_TEST_CLI` | Optional absolute installed candidate `bin/pipa.mjs`; defaults to the checkout CLI |
| `SLACK_SENDER_BOT_TOKEN` | Optional separate sender; actual posted `bot_id` must be allowed. Human token still reads channel history/replies |

`SLACK_USER_TOKEN` needs access to the selected public/private channel and the history/replies API, plus `chat:write` when used as sender. Candidate bot identity and reader/sender workspace identities must agree. The sender must pass the profile's authorization; Pipa cannot be its own test sender. Keep tokens out of command arguments, logs and child environments.

With explicit operator authorization to post test messages and create nonce routines:

```sh
node --env-file=.env.test scripts/slack-release-eval.mjs --run --mode=socket-owned
# Or only the narrower channel-destination routine smoke:
node --env-file=.env.test scripts/slack-routine-eval.mjs
```

Use `--mode=attached` with the candidate's matching `PIPA_OPENCODE_ATTACH_URL` for an attached profile. The configured engine URL is the current actual server URL; an owned replacement can bind a new port. A separately hosted attached server still needs independent deployment/ownership evidence.

The collector runs new-thread/history recall and both channel/existing-thread one-time routines serially. The shared routine flow checks preview did not mutate saved state, explicit confirmation, exact prompt, UTC/normalized one-minute schedule, route, successful scheduled lifecycle, result-session continuation, and one result after a further 35-second scheduler boundary. It deletes only newly created nonce routines and verifies their absence. It retains Slack messages for evidence and leaves the operator-owned candidate running.

Restart is separately opt-in and must be run by an observer outside the candidate's agent/process tree, on the Pipa host:

```sh
node --env-file=.env.test scripts/slack-release-eval.mjs --run --mode=socket-owned --restart
```

This posts a real restart request to the test thread. The observer checks the old generation's durable outcome, old PID exit, matching live replacement PID/generation, one exact bot-name ready notice, replacement survival, and original-session marker recall. It does not accept request acknowledgement as completion. Attached-engine PID survival, worker-exit diagnostics and post-restart scheduler recovery additionally require the native/operator checks; this collector does not certify those from a Slack reply.

Each evaluator takes a local app-scoped lock in the OS temp directory, shared across profile homes. It refuses a competing evaluator and never cancels one. If a killed evaluator leaves that lock, verify the evaluator/candidate and nonce routines before removing the stale lock manually. This lock cannot detect Socket consumers on other hosts: sole-consumer confirmation remains an operator requirement. Protected CI must also use app-scoped concurrency with `cancel-in-progress: false`.

Failed observations retain that lock: deleting currently visible nonce routines
does not prove an outstanding agent cannot create one later. Stop/drain the
candidate, reconcile every routine containing the report's nonce, verify cleanup,
then remove the retained lock. Do not launch another evaluator while this is unresolved.

Private JSON reports go under gitignored `tmp/slack-release-evals/` or `tmp/slack-routine-evals/`, mode 0600. The release collector intentionally exits nonzero with BLOCKED while human/integration gates remain unobserved, even if automated subcases pass. It records shared live case IDs, does not turn a nonce reply into `live-slack-provider` approval/file coverage, and never declares the whole release qualified. Complete the compatibility guide's private checklist and combine with required native/platform evidence. The routine-only smoke exits zero only when its own assertions and cleanup pass.

The supplied CLI and engine URL are independent probes, not proof of what the
running Socket process loaded. Reports retain the observed CLI/endpoint versions
under `identityBinding`, leave candidate package/engine/adapter unset, and mark
mode unverified. Bind the lock's PID/generation to the actual launch package,
serving endpoint and owned/attached mode in private operator evidence before
attributing automated observations to an engine cell. Repeat that binding for a
replacement. A passing probe against an unrelated v2 server cannot qualify v2
Slack behavior.

A sender bot cannot stand in for an authorized human clicking a button or submitting a modal. Use human-assisted real interaction checks where necessary and deterministic handler tests for repeatable authorization/error coverage. Mark which checks are automated and which require a responder.

Main's shipped Slack model picker remains part of the integrated behavior, not a
deferred feature. Use the [isolated model smoke](../CONTRIBUTING.md#isolated-slack-model-smoke)
to verify named/alias loading, Save/reopen/Cancel, authorization, and completed
provider/model metadata. Picker Save changes the installation default for
new/empty sessions; it does not live-switch existing threads. Verify existing
thread model retention across default changes and restart, plus immutable routine
create/preview model snapshots. Native v2 session switching/reset is a separate
executor capability and needs separate native evidence. Adapter tests alone do
not prove real Slack modal behavior or native 2.2.5 compatibility.

Run live tests sequentially by engine generation if they reuse an app. Use an app-scoped workflow concurrency lock without cancelling an active run. Paginate Slack history/replies, honor `Retry-After`, and match the exact sender/channel/thread/nonce. Validate the preview creates nothing and that the saved prompt, schedule, timezone, destination and lifecycle match the confirmed input. Keep paid/provider-backed and Slack jobs protected and manually/release-triggered; fork PRs get no secrets.

## Automatable scenarios

- A mention produces one reply; a follow-up reuses the session. Two independent threads do not block each other.
- A newer same-thread message supersedes long work without stale replies or success reactions.
- A preview leaves routine state unchanged. A confirmed one-time routine runs from the scheduler without a manual `run` request and delivers exactly one nonce result.
- Recurring runs preserve exact prompt/destination. Replies continue the result session. Deactivation/deletion and destination revocation prevent stale delivery.
- A long routine never overlaps itself; different routines can overlap. Controlled-clock tests cover DST, end dates, missed occurrences, and pending run-request recovery.
- Incoming attachment limits are checked against metadata and downloaded bytes. Both adapters accept 10 MiB and reject one byte above it; outgoing artifact limits remain separate. Measure decoded file bytes and also qualify data-URI/JSON overhead and multiple native files.
- Native 2.0.29 needs `BUN_JSC_maxRegExpStackSize=536870912` in the server process for exact 10 MiB attachments; owned v2 startup supplies it unless explicitly overridden. Configure independent attached test servers likewise. Plaintext byte-fidelity probes also need sufficient deterministic-model context to avoid testing compaction instead of attachment transport. Verify large realistic content with hashes, not a multi-megabyte substring assertion.
- Generated artifacts match expected bytes/checksums. Failed upload yields one text fallback. Unsafe paths are rejected.
- A restart requested from Slack is observed by a process outside the runtime being restarted. Verify durable outcome, old-process exit, replacement PID/generation, readiness, one ready notice, and a working follow-up.
- The replacement survives the observer/worker ending. Failed/unready replacements never report success and clean up their owned children/locks. Attached servers remain running.
- Reconnection/reload does not duplicate admitted work or delivery; pending controls are reconciled.

Use the migration plan's full feature matrix for provider/MCP/plugin/definition checks and native delegated-work compatibility. Preserve Pipa's current Slack delivery contract; testing native background execution does not introduce new acknowledgements, follow-up notifications, or background-job controls. A short nonce match alone does not establish all-feature coverage.

## Evidence and cleanup

For each scenario, record `PASS`, `FAIL`, or `BLOCKED`, versions/platform, expected and observed results, and a sanitized evidence reference. Record Slack thread/message references, session identity where relevant, duplicate counts, restart request/generation identity, and cleanup outcome.

Evidence also names the adapter selected, connection mode, package version, automated versus human-assisted coverage, and documented native `NOT_APPLICABLE` cases. Common behavior cannot be marked not applicable. Live model switching is v2-specific; ordinary v1 questions, permissions and routines are not optional.

Use a unique run nonce. Clean up only that run's test routines, files, and owned processes. Leave unrelated channel history and saved routines alone. Keep raw evidence private; share a sanitized summary. A failed cleanup makes the run fail. Missing credentials, a human responder, integration access, or platform evidence makes that coverage blocked. After collection, the operator stops the candidate, verifies process/port/lock/staging cleanup and attached-server survival, and records that separate cleanup result before relinquishing the app.

Track and close all provider/stream listeners, process trees, ports, locks, staging/artifact paths and nonce-owned routines, including failure paths. Assert an attached engine survives Pipa stop before harness-owned teardown. Keep the test root only for explicitly retained sanitized diagnostics. A local loopback server/data-URI fixture is not proof of a remote filesystem or host; separately hosted deployment coverage remains an explicit gate.

Paid/model-backed and Slack checks are opt-in commands, not unconditional CI jobs. They are still required release-qualification evidence for affected features. The implementation handoff lists every passed, failed, and blocked feature rather than claiming success from a green unit suite alone.
